terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation: with the ablative
evidence: Ov. Met. 6.354: caret ōs ūmōre loquentis
terms.comment: Cicero defines it: carēre igitur hoc significat: egēre eō quod habēre velīs, to lack means to be without what you would like to have (Tusc. 1.88). Also of what one is well without: caret perīclō, he runs no risk (Publil. Sent. C 32).

evidence: Publil. Sent. I 7: inopiae dēsunt multa
terms.comment: The noun: a lack of something, with the genitive; also poverty.

terms.grammar: verb, irregular: what is lacking is the subject, the person who lacks it in the dative
evidence: Publil. Sent. S 31: semper cōnsilium tunc deest, cum opus est maximē
Hor. Ep. 1.11.30: animus sī tē nōn dēficit aequus
terms.comment: Of what gives out: strength, time, supplies, courage.

terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation: with the ablative (or the genitive)
terms.comment: Lacking what one needs; see require.

phrases.latin: Semper cōnsilium tunc deest, cum opus est maximē.
phrases.english: Good advice is always lacking just when it is needed most.
Poverty lacks many things; greed lacks everything.

phrases.latin: caret ōs ūmōre loquentis et faucēs ārent, vixque est via vōcis in illīs
phrases.english: my mouth lacks moisture as I speak, my throat is parched, and my voice can hardly get through

phrases.latin: Quod tibi plānē deest, mī fīlī, nōn est ingenium sed ambitiō!
phrases.english: What you plainly lack, my son, is not talent but ambition!

sources: Lewis & Short: careo · Lewis & Short: inopia · Lewis & Short: desum · Lewis & Short: deficio · Lewis & Short: egeo
